sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939
sources.note: Germany invaded 1 September and Soviet forces entered eastern Poland 17 September 1939; Poland was partitioned.

sources.title: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, German Administration of Poland
sources.note: Nazi occupation, persecution and genocide of Polish Jews; Poland was partitioned between German and Soviet control in 1939.

sources.title: POLIN Museum, Popularisation of the Museum Collection
sources.note: Interwar Jewish shops, schools, synagogues, Yiddish and Sabbath life in Polish towns; the Virtual Shtetl documents local communities.

sources.title: POLIN Museum, Visions of the Jewish Future: Education, Language, and Identity
sources.note: Interwar Jewish children attended Polish state, Hebrew, Yiddish, religious and bilingual schools; the school networks had different educational and language aims.

sources.title: POLIN Museum, Core Exhibition
sources.note: Interwar Jewish cinema, café and cultural life; Holocaust and Jewish life rebuilding after 1989.

sources.title: Museum of the Second World War, Time Travel Children’s Exhibition
sources.note: Reconstructed Warsaw professional-family flat in 1939, 1943 and 1945: food substitutes, reused clothing, a displaced lodger, hidden material and clandestine lessons.

sources.title: Museum of the Second World War, Enigma and Marian Rejewski
sources.note: Rejewski and Polish Cipher Bureau colleagues deciphered Enigma; Polish intelligence passed methods to British and French counterparts in July 1939.

sources.title: Polish Government Legal Information System, Monitor Polski, 31 January 1930
sources.note: Worker-housing agreement required enough covered outdoor privies near homes and assigned upkeep; this is a regulation, not proof of universal compliance.

sources.title: POLIN Collections, Luba Blum School of Nursing
sources.note: Warsaw Jewish nursing school taught hygiene, anatomy and bacteriology; its staff later helped children under German occupation.

sources.title: European Solidarity Centre, How Did Solidarność Come To Be?
sources.note: 1980 Gdańsk Shipyard strike, Anna Walentynowicz, support from families bringing food and medicine, underground print culture and independent Solidarity trade union.

sources.title: European Solidarity Centre, Permanent Exhibition
sources.note: Strike demands, opposition, Round Table process and the 4 June 1989 elections.

sources.title: POLIN Museum, March 1968
sources.note: Communist-state antisemitic campaign forced many Polish Jews to leave in 1968.

sources.title: Sejm, Constitution of the Republic of Poland, 1997, Polish text
sources.note: Article 1 original Polish wording; constitution defines the democratic state and citizens’ rights.

European Commission, Growing Together: Poland
sources.note: Poland acceded to the European Union on 1 May 2004.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Imported poland-1920 begins approximately 1920 and has no end. It conflates the Second Republic, 1939–45 occupation, communist state and democratic republic. The label does not authenticate borders or imply one continuous regime.

Everyday examples are located in interwar Jewish communities, a Warsaw professional-family reconstruction, a farm-worker housing rule or a Gdańsk shipyard strike. They are not universal Polish conditions. Text awaits independent review.

proposedOverrides.summary: Poland regained independence in 1918. Germany and the Soviet Union invaded and partitioned it in 1939; after World War II it had shifted borders and a communist government. Solidarity and the 1989 elections helped restore democracy. The country continues, while its Jewish and other minority histories and changing borders deserve more than a single map label.
